claims.claim: The route, distance, time and date of one Thursday-morning run.
claims.evidence: Public activity: 4.83 km in 28 min 10 s on Nov 12, 2026, starting 07:04.
claims.stillLeaks: Followers-only still shows the run to every follower, including the two accounts she doesn’t recognize. Hiding the map leaves the stats visible.

claims.claim: Her very first activity shows exactly where she pressed start and stop.
claims.evidence: Run 1 (Nov 16, 2025) was uploaded before the 200 m default took effect, so its endpoints are visible.
claims.stillLeaks: Hide start/end and Hide entire map only apply to future activities. Only the address option reaches back to old runs.

claims.claim: She lives, studies or spends her mornings near Broadway & W 117th St.
claims.evidence: 141 of 141 runs start and end within 60 m of the same point (95% of starts within 27 m).
claims.stillLeaks: With Followers-only, followers still see the pattern. Any hidden circle is still centred on the place it protects.

claims.claim: Even with the 200 m default on, the hidden circle points back to the same block.
claims.evidence: Visible tracks begin 135–207 m from the true start; the average of those points is only 113 m from it.
claims.stillLeaks: A bigger hidden radius widens the circle but keeps its centre. Hide entire map works for future runs only.

claims.claim: Her elevation profile alone can help place a run in a city or borough.
claims.evidence: The run climbs from 11 m by the river to 43 m on the ridge, a profile research models have used to predict location.
claims.stillLeaks: Hiding the start/end, or a whole map, does not remove the elevation chart from the stats as far as we could confirm.

claims.claim: Which building she lives in.
claims.evidence: Her starts cluster on a campus block. Where someone presses “record” isn’t necessarily their door, and the data can’t tell the difference.

claims.claim: She runs Tuesday and Thursday mornings around 7:00, and Sunday afternoons around 3:00.
claims.evidence: 89 of 89 Tue/Thu runs start between 6:40 and 7:20; 44 of 44 Sunday runs start between 2:15 and 3:45 p.m.
claims.stillLeaks: Hiding the start time still leaves the date and weekday, so the Tue/Thu/Sun rhythm stays visible.

claims.claim: The parks and streets she passes again and again.
claims.evidence: All 141 runs go through Riverside Park or Morningside Park; route A alone appears 78 times.
claims.stillLeaks: Hide entire map is future-only; the past year of maps stays up unless each run is edited.

claims.claim: The hours she is predictably away from wherever she starts.
claims.evidence: Each run lasts about 31–50 minutes and 133 of 141 runs fall in the same three weekly slots.

claims.claim: Why she stopped running for a while.
claims.evidence: 23 days with no runs after Dec 18, 2025; 16 days with no runs after Jul 9, 2026; and only 2 runs in 11 days from May 4, 2026. These could be travel, exams, illness or a dead watch battery. The data can’t tell you which.

claims.claim: Her name, college and hometown.
claims.evidence: Shown on her fitness profile: Millie Bear · Barnard College · Brooklyn, NY.
claims.stillLeaks: Strava says Followers-only hides “certain profile details” but doesn’t list which; assume her name stays searchable.

claims.claim: Her profile can show up in search-engine results.
claims.evidence: With profile visibility set to Everyone (the default), Strava says the page “may be indexed by search engines.”
claims.stillLeaks: Search results already cached elsewhere can take time to drop out.

claims.claim: She is probably about 20 or 21.
claims.evidence: Class of 2027 at a four-year college usually means born around 2005, though people start and finish college at all ages.
claims.stillLeaks: Her class year appears on the professional profile.

claims.claim: The runner and the cognitive-science student on the professional site are the same person.
claims.evidence: 2 fields match exactly: name and college.
claims.stillLeaks: The professional profile is public on its own, and no Strava setting can change another site.

claims.claim: Her major, high school, internships and skills.
claims.evidence: Listed on the (fictional) professional profile, which anyone with a free account can view.
claims.stillLeaks: Not a Strava setting. That profile has its own visibility controls.

claims.claim: Two of her ten followers are accounts she doesn’t recognize.
claims.evidence: With profile visibility at Everyone, Strava lets anyone follow without approval.
claims.stillLeaks: Switching to Followers requires approval for new followers; existing ones stay until she removes them.

claims.claim: Her pace, distance and how often she runs.
claims.evidence: 141 runs in a year; this run averaged 5:50 /km.
claims.stillLeaks: Hidden Details can hide pace on individual runs, but not in bulk for past runs.

claims.claim: She has been getting fitter over the year.
claims.evidence: Average pace went from 6:24 /km in her first three months to 6:01 /km in her last three.

claims.claim: Her heart rate, and when and where she is working hardest.
claims.evidence: Average 154 bpm, peak 181 bpm about 1.2 km in, on the steepest climb.
claims.stillLeaks: Hiding heart rate applies to new uploads; past runs need a separate step. Strava notes hidden details “may still be visible … elsewhere in the product.”

claims.claim: Anything about a medical condition.
claims.evidence: Heart rate and pace shift with hills, heat, sleep, caffeine and the sensor itself. Nothing here establishes a diagnosis.

claims.claim: Her runs feed the public Global Heatmap by default.
claims.evidence: All 141 runs are set to Everyone, so the parts outside her hidden zones count toward the heatmap.
claims.stillLeaks: Opting out of the heatmap doesn’t change who can see her individual activities.

claims.claim: Picking her individual route out of the neighborhood heatmap.
claims.evidence: In our simulation, 91% of her weekday route lies within 15 m of at least five other runners’ tracks.
